children: is expanding its cocoa sourcing in Brazil as the food giant looks to build a more diversified and resilient supply network following sharp disruptions in the global cocoa market.

Chief Executive Officer Philipp Navratil said to Reuters in an interview that the company is working with hundreds of Brazilian farms, sharing agricultural expertise aimed at improving bean quality and farm productivity while reducing dependence on conventional fertilizers. Rising input costs, including those affected by the Middle East conflict, have increased pressure on farmers to lower production expenses.

Brazil’s cocoa industry, once a major force in global markets, was severely damaged in the 1970s by Witch’s Broom, a fungal disease that devastated plantations. Production has begun recovering as larger farms introduce tree varieties with greater resistance to the disease.
an opportunity to secure high-quality cocoa beyond its traditional dependence on West African suppliers.
The shift, however, is unlikely to quickly transform global supply. Cocoa trees can take as long as five years to reach full production.
Brazil currently produces enough cocoa largely to meet domestic demand, while the government expects national output to reach about 400,000 metric tons within five years.
Ivory Coast remains the largest producer, at roughly 2 million tons annually, followed by Ghana and an increasingly important Ecuadorian industry.

title: Nestlé expands Brazil cocoa strategy as global supplies face strain
